nodes.label: Weil restriction of a polynomial equation (GG Lemma 1)
nodes.statement: For a basis theta_1..theta_n of F_{q^n}/F_q and f in F_{q^n}[x_1..x_m], there are unique f_1..f_n in F_q[y_{i,j}] with f(sum_j y_{1,j} theta_j, ...) = sum_k theta_k f_k(y); every F_{q^n}-root (a_i) of f gives F_q-coordinates b_{i,j} with f_k(b) = 0 for all k.
nodes.scope: Elementary linear algebra over F_q; says nothing about the degree, dimension or solving cost of the descended system.
source_locations: Cohen-Frey Handbook ch. 7 (Background on Weil descent; chapter-level, unread)
non_implications: Does not bound first-fall, last-fall or solving degree of the descended summation-polynomial system.

nodes.label: Survey statement of Semaev polynomials: irreducible, degree 2^(m-2) (GG Lemma 2)
nodes.statement: For E: y^2 = x^3 + A4 x + A6 in odd characteristic, S_2 = x1 - x2, S_3 is the explicit quadratic in x3, S_m = Res_x(S_{m-j}(..., x), S_{j+2}(..., x)) for 1 <= j <= m-3; for m >= 2, S_m is an irreducible symmetric polynomial of degree 2^(m-2) in each variable. Characteristic-2 ordinary curves: S_3 = (x1x2 + x1x3 + x2x3)^2 + x1x2x3 + B.
nodes.scope: Survey restates Semaev 2004 without proof; irreducibility is attributed to Semaev and not proved in the survey.
source_locations: Semaev 2004 (ePrint 2004/031), as cited by the survey
nodes.notes: Adds the irreducibility claim and the m >= 2 range to THEOREM-SEMAEV-DEGREE (which states m >= 3 and symmetry/degree only). The proof of irreducibility for all m was not read here.

nodes.label: Heuristic #F ~ #V for subspace factor bases
nodes.statement: For F = {P in E(F_{q^n}) : x(P) in V} with V an l-dimensional F_q-subspace, practice assumes #F ~ #V = q^l; nonemptiness and generation of the group are separate questions with only partial results (Diem 2011 Props. 4.11 and 4.29, Kohel-Shparlinski, Kosters, Shparlinski-Voloch).
nodes.scope: Extension fields F_{q^n}, n >= 2; the survey labels it explicitly as a heuristic assumption.
failure_modes: V chosen so that x-coordinates in V rarely lift to F_{q^n}-points

nodes.label: Decomposable proportion ~1/n! (l=1) or q^(lk-n)/k!
nodes.statement: With k = n, l = 1, 'taking symmetries into account and assuming there are no unexpected cancellations' the number of n-sums from F is ~ q^n/n!, so a random point decomposes with probability ~1/n!; for an l-dimensional V the probability is ~ q^(lk-n)/k!.
nodes.scope: Counting heuristic over extension fields; the survey states it as 'should be roughly'.
source_locations: Galbraith-Gaudry 2016, Section 8, 'Dimension-1 factor base' and 'Higher dimension factor base'
nodes.formula: Pr[decompose] ~ q^(l k - n) / k!  (l = 1, k = n: 1/n!)

nodes.label: Survey statement: O~(q^2), O~(q^(2-2/n)) for fixed n
nodes.statement: For E over F_{q^n} with n fixed and q growing, a heuristic analysis 'as in Gaudry' assumes polynomial-time system solving for fixed n, giving O~(q) per needed relations and O~(q^2) overall; the double-large-prime variation gives heuristic O~(q^(2-2/n)).
nodes.scope: The survey calls both figures heuristic running times; constants in n are exponential and not given.
nodes.formula: O~(q^2); O~(q^(2-2/n)) with double large primes

nodes.label: Survey report of Diem's rigorous L(2/3) sequence
nodes.statement: Diem proved there is a sequence of prime powers Q_i = q_i^(n_i), with n_i on the order of sqrt(log q_i), such that ECDLP in E(F_{Q_i}) for every elliptic curve over F_{Q_i} is solvable in rigorous subexponential time L_{Q_i}(2/3); Diem 2013 extended the range to n up to about log q using higher-dimensional factor bases.
nodes.scope: As reported by the survey; the exact n_i(q_i) relation is rendered with a broken radical in the HAL PDF and should be checked in Diem 2011.
source_locations: Galbraith-Gaudry 2016, Section 8, end of 'Dimension-1 factor base'
non_implications: Says nothing about E(F_{2^n}) with n prime (the survey states these results 'shed no light' on that case).

nodes.label: No efficient decomposition for prime-field small-abscissa factor base
nodes.statement: For E over F_p, Semaev's factor base of points with small integer abscissa has no known efficient decomposition algorithm because the group law is 'deeply incompatible' with integer multiplication of abscissae; prime-field curves 'remain unaffected by index calculus'.
nodes.scope: State of knowledge in Aug 2015; the survey does not discuss the algebraic prime-field route of Petit-Kosters-Messeng (PKC 2016).

nodes.label: Survey definition of the First Fall Degree Assumption
nodes.statement: The first fall degree is, roughly, the degree F4/F5 is handling when a degree fall first occurs; 'it has been observed that this degree is often not too far from the maximal degree that will ever occur', and the FFDA is the assumption that this holds for the ECDLP systems.
nodes.scope: Informal description, explicitly 'roughly speaking'; algorithm- and order-dependent as described.

nodes.label: No consensus on subexponential ECDLP over F_(2^n) (GG Sec. 10.2)
nodes.statement: As of 2015 'there is no consensus whether there is a subexponential algorithm for ECDLP in characteristic 2'; 'the FFDA approach seems to be too optimistic, while the LFD approach looks more precise, but much harder to estimate'; no approach is practical for any key size in use even under the most optimistic assumptions, and small experiments cannot (in)validate the assumptions (strong law of small numbers).
nodes.scope: Survey assessment; proposed next steps: prove the LFD for ECDLP systems, find a new notion, or a new solving strategy.
source_locations: Galbraith-Gaudry 2016, Section 1 (authors' belief that F_(2^n), n prime, curves are not threatened)

nodes.label: Semaev 2015 unrolled-resultant subexponential conjecture (as surveyed)
nodes.statement: Experiments with the unrolled (splitting) system led Semaev (ePrint 2015/310) to conjecture a subexponential algorithm; depending on the variant and 'how much one is ready to believe', researchers conjectured L_{2^n}(2/3) or even L_{2^n}(1/2) for ECDLP in E(F_{2^n}). The survey: 'this conjecture is not yet demonstrated to our satisfaction'.
nodes.scope: Binary fields; rests on first-fall-degree style assumptions for the unrolled system.

nodes.label: Unrolled-resultant (splitting) decomposition system
nodes.statement: Replace S_{k+1}(x_1..x_k, x_R) by the chain S_3(x_1,x_2,T_1)=0, S_3(T_1,x_3,T_2)=0, ..., S_3(T_{k-2},x_k,x_R)=0 with k-2 auxiliary variables over F_{q^n}; after Weil descent with x_i in an l-dimensional V the system has n(k-1) equations in kl + (k-2)n variables of low degree, versus n equations in kl variables of degree growing like 2^(k-1).
nodes.scope: Trade of degree for variables; equal equation/variable counts when kl = n.

nodes.label: Symmetric coordinates need V closed under products
nodes.statement: Rewriting S_{m+1} in elementary symmetric e_i reduces solutions by m! and can lower degree (S_3: total degree 4 -> 3), but after restricting x_i to V the e_i stay in an l-dimensional space only if the products V^(i) span a space of the same dimension (e.g. V a subfield); otherwise the e_i (i >= 2) range over a larger span and the number of descended variables grows.
nodes.scope: Elementary observation; the survey adds that with the Huang-Petit-Shinohara-Takagi choice of V 'there is no doubt that the number of variables increases significantly', and that Galbraith-Gebregiyorgis found the combined ideas not competitive with Pollard rho.
non_implications: Does not quantify the variable growth for a given V.

nodes.label: Right-kernel IC needs full rank, rarely met at #relations = #F
nodes.statement: Left-kernel (target-dependent) relations are 'much easier to analyze rigorously'. Right-kernel (target-independent) relations yield all factor-base logs only if the matrix has rank #F - 1, which 'is rarely verified if we have just as many relations as the number of unknowns', so practice collects many more relations; Pomerance gave relation-generation techniques that force the rank condition (in F_p^*).
nodes.scope: General index calculus; the extra-relation margin is heuristic for elliptic-curve factor bases.
source_locations: Galbraith-Gaudry 2016, Section 6.1 (sparse linear algebra: Joux 2009, Section 3.4; unread)

nodes.label: GHS fails in general: cover genus exponential in n
nodes.statement: GHS-type covers succeed only for a few families; 'in general this approach fails, because the curves C that are constructed have a genus that is exponential in n instead of linear in n'; the systematic odd-characteristic classification of Iijima-Momose-Chao (ePrint 2015/805) shows 'there is not so much to expect anymore'.
nodes.scope: Survey assessment summarising the GHS genus formula and later classifications; 'in general' is not quantified over a curve distribution.
source_locations: Blake-Seroussi-Smart 2005 ch. VIII (Hess, Weil descent attacks), pp. 151-180, unread

nodes.label: Speeding up index calculus on subfield (Koblitz) curves is open
nodes.statement: Using Frobenius on a subfield curve to raise relation probability, or to obtain many relations per system solution, is 'a major open problem'; Gorla-Massierer's trace-zero-variety index calculus 'does not currently lead to a dramatic speed-up'.
nodes.scope: Index calculus only; rho on subfield curves already gains sqrt(2n) from Frobenius orbits.

nodes.label: Disjoint factor bases: expected (k-1)! gain
nodes.statement: Requiring P_i in disjoint factor bases F_i removes the k! loss in success probability at the price of k times as many unknowns and relations, so 'one might therefore expect an overall speedup by a factor of (k-1)!' (Matsuo idea; analysed by Galbraith-Gebregiyorgis).
nodes.scope: Expected-value heuristic; interacts with invariant-coordinate choices.

nodes.label: Over-/under-determined decomposition trade-off
nodes.statement: Decreasing k below the square choice gives over-determined systems that solve much faster but divide the success probability by #F per decrement (Joux-Vitse, F_{p^5}); it is most effective when only one decomposition is needed, e.g. oracle-assisted static-DH attacks (Granger). Increasing k gives positive-dimensional systems whose generic Groebner basis enables sieving (Joux-Vitse) but is usually too large.
nodes.scope: Survey summary; profitability is instance-dependent and not proven asymptotically.

nodes.label: BSGS O(sqrt r) 'optimal due to Shoup's lower bound'
nodes.statement: BSGS uses O(sqrt r) group operations and O(sqrt r) storage, and this asymptotic complexity 'is optimal due to Shoup's lower bound' for generic algorithms; Pollard's interleaving gives average (4/3)sqrt r, and with x-coordinate matching on E the average is (4/3)sqrt(r/2) ~ 0.943 sqrt r.
nodes.scope: Optimality holds in the generic group model only; the survey's sentence names generic algorithms.
non_implications: No statement about non-generic algorithms on a specific curve.

cited_by.note: Cites the survey (as 'DCC 2015') for O(sqrt n) optimality and correctly scopes it to the generic model.

nodes.label: Best-possible BSGS constant and grumpy-giants running time
nodes.statement: In the Chateauneuf-Ling-Stinson model (an 'unrealistic' model where any aP + bQ costs one operation) a single list gives worst case (sqrt 2 + o(1)) sqrt r and average ~(0.943 + o(1)) sqrt r, about (2/3 + o(1)) sqrt r average with inversion; Bernstein-Lange 'two grumpy giants and a baby' is heuristically ~(1.2 + o(1)) sqrt r average, with no precise statement proved. Determining its exact average-case time and approaching the lower bound is open.
nodes.scope: Generic algorithms; the lower-bound model is not Shoup's query model.

nodes.label: Rho/kangaroo analyses are heuristic; worst case unbounded
nodes.statement: Pollard rho with distinguished points has heuristic serial average (sqrt(pi/2) + o(1)) sqrt r group operations; 'it is natural to believe that this running time is optimal' among collision methods; worst-case running time is unbounded; 'most papers on the Pollard rho and kangaroo algorithms rely on heuristic assumptions' (partition count: Brent-Pollard, Blackburn-Murphy, Bernstein-Lange; rigorous results by Kijima-Montenegro and Montenegro et al.). Variance is large, so expected time is a guideline only over many instances.
nodes.scope: Generic walks on E; negation/Frobenius orbits handled separately.

nodes.label: Negation-map speedup: practical dispute recorded
nodes.statement: Rho on orbits of an automorphism of average orbit size l 'should be sped up by approximately sqrt(l)'; Bos-Kleinjung-Lenstra raised fruitless-cycle overheads suggesting the speedup could be less than sqrt(l); Bernstein-Lange-Schwabe showed how to organise the computation to minimise these concerns.
nodes.scope: Survey records both positions without a final quantitative verdict.

nodes.label: Multi-target ECDLP: total sqrt(rL), not L sqrt(r)
nodes.statement: L instances Q_i = a_i P in one group of prime order r (L <= r) can be solved with O(sqrt(rL)) group operations in total: deterministically by BSGS with a shared baby-step table of size sqrt(rL) and sqrt(r/L) giant steps per target; heuristically by rho retaining distinguished points (Kuhn-Struik: about sqrt(2rL) for L < r^(1/4)). The amortised cost per key falls like sqrt(r/L).
nodes.scope: Solving all L targets. It does not speed up finding the first of L keys (see OPEN-BK-GG-ONE-OUT-OF-L).
source_locations: SafeCurves rho.html, 'Does rho become cheaper against multiple targets?'
nodes.formula: total O(sqrt(r L)); Kuhn-Struik ~ sqrt(2 r L) for L < r^(1/4)
nodes.notes: The BSGS variant is the elementary balancing M + L r / M at M = sqrt(rL); stated here because it makes the refutation of CLAIM-BK-X962-NO-AMORTIZATION rigorous rather than heuristic.

cited_by.note: check_multi_target_margin uses per-key bits 0.5*(log2 n - log2 m), which matches the amortised all-keys cost, but its comment attributes it to 'Galbraith-Lin-Scott' (the literature attribution is Kuhn-Struik 2001) and claims one walk solves 'any one of them' in O(sqrt(n/m)), which neither survey supports; see OPEN-BK-GG-ONE-OUT-OF-L.

nodes.label: ANSI X9.62 (1997): effort must be repeated per key
nodes.statement: ANSI X9.62 (1997), as quoted by SafeCurves: 'the computation of a single elliptic curve discrete logarithm has the effect of revealing a single user's private key. The same effort must be repeated in order to determine another user's private key.'
nodes.scope: Quoted standard text; X9.62 itself was not read.
source_locations: SafeCurves rho.html, multi-target paragraph (quotation of ANSI X9.62, 1997)
nodes.notes: SafeCurves: 'The second sentence is incorrect: the effort is reduced for each subsequent key.'

nodes.label: Yun: generic Omega(sqrt(rL)) for L-instance DLP
nodes.statement: Kuhn and Struik conjectured an Omega(sqrt(rL)) lower bound for solving L ECDLP instances in one group; Yun (EUROCRYPT 2015) proved it in the generic group model.
nodes.scope: Generic model; reported by the survey, paper unread.

nodes.label: One-out-of-L ECDLP: no speedup known
nodes.statement: For the 'one out of L' problem (solve any one of L instances in the same group) the survey is 'not aware of any algorithm that solves that problem in less time than a single ECDLP instance'; SafeCurves likewise states the first key found still costs ~0.886 sqrt(l) additions because success after m additions is still ~m^2/l.
nodes.scope: Neither source proves a lower bound for this problem.
source_locations: SafeCurves rho.html, 'Does rho become faster against the first of multiple targets?'

cited_by.note: Comment on attack 8 says a single rho walk can solve 'any one' of m keys in O(sqrt(n/m)); both surveys say no such algorithm is known. The proposed mitigation (a fresh base point per key in the same group) does not prevent amortisation, since the attacker can take logs of every base point and key to one common generator (2m instances).

nodes.label: Precomputation: r^(1/3) per instance after r^(2/3) (Bernstein-Lange)
nodes.statement: Ignoring precomputation cost, one can heuristically solve each ECDLP instance in O(r^(1/3)) group operations after an O(r^(2/3)) precomputation with a program of O(r^(1/3) log r) bits (Bernstein-Lange 2012/2013; also Lee-Cheon-Hong, Hong-Lee); the survey notes a full table of logs does not fit since its program is O(r log r) bits.
nodes.scope: Non-uniform/precomputation model; the survey declines to discuss interpretations.
nodes.formula: online O(r^(1/3)), precomputation O(r^(2/3)), advice O(r^(1/3) log r) bits

nodes.label: Cheon / Brown-Gallant cost O(max(sqrt(r/d), sqrt d))
nodes.statement: Given P, aP, a^d P with P of order r and d | r - 1, a is found in O(max{sqrt(r/d), sqrt d}) group operations; with d ~ r^(1/2) this is O(r^(1/4)) (the survey prints O(p^(1/4))); a variant handles d | r + 1.
nodes.scope: Requires the auxiliary input a^d P (or a static-DH oracle supplying it).
source_locations: SEC 1 v2.0, Appendix B.1 (Cheon via static DH: about n^(1/3) computation and n^(1/3) oracle invocations when n-1 or n+1 has a factor near n^(1/3))
nodes.notes: Survey typo: 'O(p^(1/4))' where the setting is r; for prime-order curves r ~ p by Hasse, so the exponent is unaffected.

nodes.label: Mapping ECDLP to an isogenous curve is generally efficient
nodes.statement: By Galbraith's algorithm (improved by Galbraith-Hess-Smart) 'it is generally possible to efficiently map a discrete logarithm problem in an elliptic curve E to another E' in the same isogeny class where the problem might be easier to solve' (see also Jao-Miller-Venkatesan).
nodes.scope: 'Generally' and 'efficiently' rest on expected-time isogeny-path heuristics, not stated in the survey.

nodes.label: AG-code minimum distance vs ECDLP (survey says 'equivalent')
nodes.statement: One can construct algebraic-geometry codes from elliptic curves such that computing the minimum distance of the code is equivalent to solving the ECDLP (Driencourt-Michon 1987; rediscovered by Cheng 2008); Augot-Morain explored solving ECDLP this way, 'so far ... not very promising'.
nodes.scope: Reported by the survey; the direction(s) of the reduction were not checked in the primary papers.
nodes.notes: Cheng's title ('Hard problems of algebraic geometry codes') suggests ECDLP <= minimum distance (a hardness transfer to coding); the survey's word 'equivalent' may overstate. Needs the primary text.

nodes.label: Brauer-group, signature-calculus and Kolyvagin routes: no practical impact
nodes.statement: Frey's Brauer-group formulation, Huang-Raskind signature calculus and the (unpublished) Rubin-Silverberg Kolyvagin-system transfer 'reveal deep connections' but none 'has been demonstrated to have any practical impact'; xedni calculus was analysed by Jacobson et al. as 'not likely to be successful'.
nodes.scope: Survey assessment as of 2015.

nodes.label: CDH: only known method is solving ECDLP
nodes.statement: 'Currently the only known way to solve the Computational Diffie-Hellman problem is to solve the ECDLP'; DDH is easy via pairings for special curves but otherwise needs ECDLP; hence ECDLP study 'is the main way to assess the security' of EC applications.
nodes.scope: State-of-knowledge statement; does not assert a reduction CDH -> DLP.

nodes.label: Generic lower-bound gap for l-SDH proved real by Cheon
nodes.statement: Boneh-Boyen proved l-SDH needs about sqrt(p/l) operations in a generic group with pairing, weaker by sqrt(l) than DL; the gap was first thought 'an artifact of the proof', but Cheon's attack (the Brown-Gallant method) recovers x in about sqrt(p/l0) operations when l0 <= l divides p - 1 and l0 < p^(1/3), so in some cases p^(1/3). Koblitz-Menezes conclude group order bitlength must grow ~50% for the same guarantee.
nodes.scope: Non-standard (auxiliary-input) assumptions; DL itself is unaffected.
source_locations: Koblitz-Menezes 2007 (Another look at generic groups), abstract only
non_implications: Does not show any slack in Shoup's sqrt(p) bound for DL itself.

nodes.label: Oracle-relative DL assumptions (all-primes-but-p) are easier than DL
nodes.statement: Koblitz-Menezes restate the 'all-primes-but-p' and 'one-prime-not-p' discrete-log problems (DL in a group of order p given an oracle for DL in groups of other prime orders) and give evidence that they are strictly easier than DL; they warn that assumptions treating DL in different groups as independent 'should be used with caution'.
nodes.scope: Evidence rather than a reduction; Remarks 8-9 discuss why such assumptions are not self-contradictory.

nodes.label: SEC 1 v2.0 domain-parameter validation (B < 100, n != p)
nodes.statement: SEC 1 v2.0 validation over F_p requires (among others) n prime, h <= 2^(t/8), h = floor((sqrt p + 1)^2 / n), nG = O, and p^B != 1 mod n for all 1 <= B < 100 together with n != p; step 8 'excludes the known weak classes' susceptible to MOV, Frey-Rueck or Semaev-Smart-Satoh-Araki.
nodes.scope: Prime-field validation primitive; security level t in {80,112,128,192,256}.

nodes.label: SEC 1 v2.0 ECDLP hardness narrative
nodes.statement: 'No general subexponential algorithms are known for the ECDLP'; best general algorithms are rho (sqrt(pi n/2), or sqrt(pi n/4) with negation) and lambda (2 sqrt n); Frobenius on F_{2^(ed)} curves defined over F_{2^e} gives sqrt(2d), e.g. Koblitz curve over F_{2^163} at about 2^77 versus 2^81 steps; three special classes are weak (small MOV degree B, anomalous, composite-degree binary fields by Weil descent/index calculus, 'should be avoided' as a precaution); 'All known weak classes of curves are excluded in this document.' The MOV bound B >= 20 'was updated to B >= 100 in [X9.62a]'.
nodes.scope: Standard commentary as of 2009, before the 2012-2015 binary summation-polynomial work.
source_locations: SEC 1 cites HMV04, BSS99, BSS05, GM05, CFA+06 for ECDLP difficulty (chapter-level, unread)

nodes.label: SEC 1: a slightly larger cofactor makes ECDH roughly as hard as DLP
nodes.statement: SEC 1 v2.0 states that Brown and Gallant argue a slightly larger cofactor 'may provide' a theoretical benefit: 'given a cofactor of a certain size, it can be shown that breaking the elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman primitive is roughly as difficult as solving the discrete logarithm problem'.
nodes.scope: Stated without hypotheses or a reference to a theorem number; Brown-Gallant (ePrint 2004/306) not read.
source_locations: SEC 1 v2.0, Appendix B.1, p. 71 (Cheon/Brown-Gallant paragraph)
nodes.notes: Phrased as an established result ('it can be shown') though the conditions are not given; equivalence results known to this corpus (den Boer, Maurer) are conditional on auxiliary group orders.

nodes.label: Brainpool (RFC 5639) security requirements
nodes.statement: RFC 5639 requires: (1) (q-1)/l < 100 where l is the order of p mod q (embedding degree near maximal; excludes supersingular); (2) trace != 1; (3) class number of the maximal order of End(E) (x) Q larger than 10^7; (4) prime group order (cofactor 1); (5) verifiably pseudo-random generation; (6) a proof that the requirements are met.
nodes.scope: Prime-field curves; described as 'a restrictive position' that 'may be sensible to slightly deviate from' for performance.

nodes.label: Large class number as a guard against lifting
nodes.statement: RFC 5639 motivates the class-number bound by: 'Generally, E cannot be lifted to a curve E' over an algebraic number field L with End(E) = End(E') unless the degree of L over the rationals is larger than the class number of End(E)'; it concedes 'there are no efficient attacks exploiting a small class number' and cites Jao-Miller-Venkatesan and Hess-Rueck-type work only as 'argument for' the condition.
nodes.scope: Defensive rationale; no attack is claimed. The degree statement is CM theory (j of a CM lift generates the ring class field), stated loosely ('generally', 'larger than').

nodes.label: NIST SP 800-186: no technical rationale for a |Disc| bound
nodes.statement: For trace t, Disc = t^2 - 4q is closely related to the discriminant of the endomorphism field; 'there is no technical rationale for imposing a large lower bound on the square-free part of |Disc|' and the Recommendation imposes none. Other C.1 criteria: field prime or 2^m with m prime; cofactor h <= 2^10; |E| != q; embedding degree k >= 2^10.
nodes.scope: Recommended curves; binary-field curves are listed but deprecated for 'limited adoption' (Section 3.3), not for a cryptanalytic reason.
source_locations: NIST SP 800-186, Section 3.3 and Table 2 (binary curves deprecated)

nodes.label: NIST: security strength ~ half the bit length of n
nodes.statement: 'The security strength of an elliptic curve is directly related to the order of the basepoint. In general, if an elliptic curve has a basepoint of order n, then the security strength will be approximately one half of the bit length of n' (Table 1: 112 for P-224, K-233, B-233; 128 for P-256, Curve25519, Edwards25519, K-283, B-283; etc.).
nodes.scope: Classical generic-attack accounting; automorphism speedups (Frobenius on K-curves) are absorbed by 'approximately'.

nodes.label: SafeCurves rho rule: l >= 2^200 (0.886 sqrt l > 2^100)
nodes.statement: Rho breaks ECDLP using on average about 0.886 sqrt(l) = sqrt(pi/4) sqrt(l) 'batched affine' short-Weierstrass additions (negation included); SafeCurves requires l >= 2^200 so that rho costs above 2^100, and imposes the same ECDLP requirements on the twist ('twist rho').
nodes.scope: Prime-field curves; the 2^100 floor is justified by a 1/2^20 success probability after 2^90 additions.

nodes.label: SafeCurves transfer rule: embedding degree >= (l-1)/100
nodes.statement: SafeCurves calls the SEC/X9.62/P1363 small-threshold approach 'risky' ('the point of ECC has always been to avoid index calculus') and adopts the Brainpool-style 'overkill' requirement that the embedding degree be at least (l-1)/100; it also excludes l = p (additive transfer).
nodes.scope: Pairing-based cryptography explicitly out of scope.

nodes.label: SafeCurves: 'SEC1 requires the embedding degree to be at least 20'
nodes.statement: SafeCurves transfer.html states that SEC1 and X9.62 require the embedding degree to be at least 20, and P1363 never more than 30.
nodes.scope: Description of other standards; versions not named on the page (2013.10.13).
source_locations: SafeCurves transfer.html, 'Standards vary in the requirements...'
nodes.notes: Refuted as a description of SEC 1 v2.0 (2009), whose validation step 8 rejects every B < 100 and whose Appendix B.1 says the 20 bound was raised to 100 in X9.62a. It may describe SEC 1 v1.0 (2000) or the original X9.62 (1998); those were not read.

nodes.label: SafeCurves discriminant rule: |D| > 2^100
nodes.statement: SafeCurves requires the CM field discriminant D (from t^2 - 4p) to satisfy |D| > 2^100, while stating that small |D| only enables known, 'reasonably well understood' endomorphism speedups of rho, 'there is no evidence of serious problems with either small |D| or large |D|', and 'it is also conceivable that curves with large |D| are much easier to break'.
nodes.scope: Precautionary rule, explicitly not attack-driven.

nodes.label: SafeCurves: Brainpool class number must exceed 1000000
nodes.statement: SafeCurves disc.html: 'Brainpool contains a related requirement: the class number ... is required to be larger than 1000000', and (under GRH, class number ~ sqrt|D|) this is much weaker than |D| > 2^100.
nodes.scope: Description of the Brainpool standard.
nodes.notes: RFC 5639 Section 2.1(3) states 10^7, not 10^6. The 2005 Brainpool document was not read. SafeCurves' comparative conclusion survives either way (2^50 >> 10^7).

nodes.label: SafeCurves twist-security rule (>= 2^100 combined attack)
nodes.statement: For x-only ladders where Bob neither multiplies by the cofactors h, h' nor checks curve membership, the combined small-subgroup brute force on the twist plus kangaroo on the remaining l/(h h' ...) possibilities must cost at least 2^100; all ECDLP requirements are also imposed on the twist (example: twist cofactor primes near 2^8, 2^18, 2^90 leave a 2^82 kangaroo attack).
nodes.scope: Implementation-boundary criterion; a curve designer can remove the exposure, an implementer can remove it by validation.

nodes.label: Standards disagree on the MOV/embedding-degree threshold
nodes.statement: Published thresholds differ by orders of magnitude and none is derived from a stated finite-field DLP cost model: SEC 1 v2.0 rejects B < 100 (formerly 20); NIST SP 800-186 requires k >= 2^10; Brainpool requires (q-1)/k < 100, i.e. k within a factor 100 of maximal; SafeCurves adopts the Brainpool-style bound and reports SEC1/X9.62 as 20; P1363 (per SafeCurves) never more than 30. Likewise for the CM discriminant: SafeCurves |D| > 2^100, Brainpool class number > 10^7, NIST none ('no technical rationale').
nodes.scope: Comparison of standards texts read on 2026-11-02; P1363 and X9.62 not read.
source_locations: SEC 1 v2.0, Section 3.1.1.2.1 step 8 and Appendix B.1

cited_by.note: AnalysisOptions defaults flag MOV only for k <= 6 (search to 100), far below every standard's threshold (SEC1 100, NIST 2^10, Brainpool/SafeCurves (n-1)/100), and no CM-discriminant check exists.

research_targets.label: Derive embedding-degree and discriminant thresholds from cost
research_targets.objective: Replace the four incompatible standards thresholds (SEC 1 B >= 100, NIST k >= 2^10, Brainpool/SafeCurves (l-1)/k < 100; CM |D| > 2^100 vs class number > 10^7 vs none) with a derivation from current F_{p^k} DLP cost estimates, and decide whether src/ecc_safety.rs's k <= 6 MOV flag is defensible.
research_targets.acceptance: A table giving, for log2 p in {256, 384, 521} and k = 1..k_max, the best published F_{p^k} DLP cost with source, and the smallest k for which it exceeds sqrt(l); each standard's threshold placed against it; ecc_safety defaults either justified or changed in a separate PR.
research_targets.next_step: Collect current TNFS/NFS cost estimates for F_{p^k} (pairing-cluster sources) and compute the crossover k per field size.

research_targets.label: Settle one-out-of-L ECDLP and fix the repository's multi-target check
research_targets.objective: Find or prove a generic lower bound for solving any one of L ECDLP instances (both surveys say no speedup is known), and correct src/ecc_safety.rs, which claims one rho walk solves 'any one' of m keys in O(sqrt(n/m)), attributes amortised rho to 'Galbraith-Lin-Scott', and proposes per-key generators as a mitigation.
research_targets.acceptance: A cited generic-model bound (or proof) for 1-out-of-L, and an ecc_safety.rs comment and check whose model (all keys amortised vs first key) matches it.
research_targets.next_step: Search for generic bounds on 1-out-of-m DLP (e.g. post-Yun generalized-DLP lower bounds) and read the primary text.

research_targets.label: Inventory the ECDLP chapters of the standard textbooks
research_targets.objective: Do for Cohen-Frey Handbook ch. 19-22, Hankerson-Menezes-Vanstone Section 4.1, Blake-Seroussi-Smart 1999 ch. V and 2005 ch. VIII-IX, and Washington ch. 5 what galbraith-2018-inventory.json does for Galbraith 2018: list every numbered result, and flag where a heuristic (rho random mapping, decomposition probability, FFDA, relation rank) is stated as a theorem.
research_targets.acceptance: Per-book inventory with chapter/section/theorem/page locators and a SHA-256 of the copy read; each flagged statement linked to the corpus node it overstates.
research_targets.next_step: Obtain licensed copies (the books are not openly available; only chapter lists were verified here).

research_targets.label: Measure #F vs #V and the 1/n! decomposable proportion
research_targets.objective: Test the two counting heuristics the fixed-n estimates rest on (#F ~ q^l; Pr[decompose] ~ q^(lk-n)/k!) by exhaustive counts on small extension-field curves, including subspaces V that are not subfields.
research_targets.acceptance: Exact counts for a preregistered grid (q, n, l, k) with the ratio to the heuristic and its spread across curves; any systematic deviation reported with the V construction that causes it.
research_targets.next_step: Freeze the grid and curve sampler under the controlled-experiment protocol; reuse the repository's exact decomposition counters.

research_targets.objective: Read Driencourt-Michon 1987 and Cheng 2008 and record which direction(s) of the reduction are proved and under what code parameters.
